prompt: Some people believe that newspapers and websites should be free to publish stories about the private lives of famous people. Others think that famous people have the same right to privacy as anyone else. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Both sides of this argument treat fame as the deciding factor: one holds that celebrity is a bargain in which privacy is the price, the other that a famous person remains a person. Each captures something true, but fame seems to me the wrong test. Whether a private fact may be published should depend on whether it bears on a role its subject holds in public, and on that basis many famous people deserve more protection than they receive, while some obscure ones deserve less.

The case for freedom to publish is strongest where power is involved. A minister who conceals a financial interest in a company his department regulates, or a magistrate whose private dealings call her impartiality into question, has a private life that is also a public matter, and a press forbidden to report it would be failing in its most important function. The bargain argument has some force too. A celebrity who sells magazines an idealised picture of family life, and earns endorsements from it, can hardly object when the picture is exposed as false, because the falsehood was part of what was sold.

The case for privacy is strongest everywhere else, which is to say in most of what is actually published. An actor's illness, a footballer's divorce and photographs of a singer's children on the way to school inform the public of nothing that affects it; they are interesting to the public rather than in the public interest, and the distinction is not a technicality. The person pursued pays in anxiety, strained relationships and the loss of any ordinary life, and relatives who never chose publicity pay alongside them.

My own view, then, is that neither position should be accepted whole. Public figures surrender privacy only in the areas their public role touches: a politician's finances, a campaigner's consistency with the cause they promote, a celebrity's honesty about whatever they have chosen to sell. Beyond those areas fame confers no licence to intrude, and a rule built on that principle would protect most famous people while leaving the press free to do the reporting that genuinely matters.
title: Reporting on the private lives of the famous
